EIGE SINGLE PROGRAMMING DOCUMENT 2026–2028
Foreword
The European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE) upholds its reputation as the knowledge centre for
gender equality in the EU. Policymakers across Europe continue to rely on the Agency’s expert knowledge
and resources to inform decision-making. EIGE’s data and evidence are essential to help Europe’s leaders to
design measures that are inclusive and promote gender equality in all areas of life, especially amid
technological and climate change, the changing nature of work and widening inequalities, the increasing
influence of new governing systems, backlash against progress towards gender equality, new security
challenges and the cost-of-living crisis.
This single programming document covers 2026–2028. EIGE’s work in this period and in the years to come
will be greatly influenced by the outcomes of the European elections in 2024, resulting in new strategic
political priorities, such as those set in the EU strategic agenda and the Commission priorities for 2024–
2029, which includes a new gender equality strategy for 2026–2030 and a roadmap for women’s rights.
EIGE’s priorities will be closely aligned with those of the EU for achieving gender equality across different
policy areas.
Throughout 2026–2028, EIGE will continue to support the presidencies of the Council of the European
Union to monitor the EU’s international gender equality commitments. This will include reviewing progress
in gender equality within the first-semester presidencies’ priority areas outlined in the Beijing Platform for
Action, and providing evidence on EU policy priorities for the second-semester presidencies. EIGE’s Gender
Equality Index, the EU’s benchmarking and monitoring tool for gender equality, will continue to serve as an
annual barometer of the state of gender equality in the EU. The results of EIGE’s second CARE Survey of
Gender Gaps in Unpaid Care, Individual and Social Activities will allow monitoring of EU commitments in
the areas of gender equality, social rights and care.
EIGE’s work on gender mainstreaming will focus on developing evidence-based practical resources and
providing policy support and technical assistance to help policymakers at the EU and national levels integrate
a gender perspective into all policy areas and stages of the policymaking cycle. EIGE will provide tailored and
demand-driven support for gender mainstreaming and update the policy areas section in the Gender
Mainstreaming Platform. EIGE will continue to provide the EU with the latest sex-disaggregated data and
gender statistics for a range of policy areas, and quality standards for gender statistics within its Gender
Statistics Database.
Elimination of gender-based violence will remain one of the main EU priorities and the core of EIGE’s
activities. EIGE has established itself as a primary source of information and tools to support the EU
Member States in their responses to violence against women. In 2026–2028, EIGE will continue to
standardise data and make it comparable, and establish a coordination system for its collection in the EU to
support monitoring of the EU directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence.
EIGE will communicate key messages on gender equality by means of campaigns and through a variety of
channels and outreach to its key stakeholders. EIGE will also organise its third Gender Equality Forum in
2026.
Data and evidence are the bedrock of informed and effective policymaking on gender equality. I believe that
this work programme provides plentiful and fertile grounds for developing policies across all different areas
of life.
Carlien Scheele

Mission statement
Gender equality is a fundamental value of the EU. It is enshrined in the treaties (Article 2 and Article 3(3) of
the Treaty on European Union and Article 8 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) and
the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (2009). Article 23 of the charter states that
‘Equality between women and men must be ensured in all areas, including employment, work and pay. The
principle of equality shall not prevent the maintenance or adoption of measures providing for specific
advantages in favour of the under-represented sex.’
Regulation (EU) No 1922/2006 establishing a European Institute for Gender Equality (Founding Regulation)
sets out the mandate and objectives of the European Institute for Gender Equality (1). The Founding
Regulation states that ‘The overall objectives of the Institute shall be to contribute to and strengthen the
promotion of gender equality, including gender mainstreaming in all Community policies and the resulting
national policies, and the fight against discrimination based on sex, and to raise EU citizens’ awareness of
gender equality by providing technical assistance to the Community institutions, in particular the
Commission, and the authorities of the Member States as set out in Article 3.’

EIGE’s mission is as follows.
To be the European knowledge centre on gender equality
We are an independent knowledge centre and the primary source of information on gender
equality in the EU. We contribute to making the EU become a union of equality, where women
and men, girls and boys in all their diversity are free to pursue their chosen path in life, have equal
opportunities to thrive and can equally participate in and lead our societies.
EIGE’s unique expert knowledge, research, data and tools help policymakers to design measures
that are inclusive and transformative and promote gender equality in all areas of life. We
communicate our expertise effectively and work closely with partners to raise awareness at the
EU and national levels, and in EU candidate countries and potential candidate countries.
To support the promotion of gender equality in the EU we:
• provide research and collect and analyse data on gender equality with an intersectional
perspective;
• develop methods to improve gender statistics and data collections;
• communicate our comparable and reliable data and information with a hope-based
approach;
• measure the state of gender equality at both the EU and Member State levels;
• develop methodological tools and provide technical support for gender mainstreaming in
all EU and national policies;
• cooperate with EU institutions, Member States, international organisations, non-
governmental organisations, equal opportunities’ organisations, universities and experts,
research centres, social partners and related bodies, the media and our EU sister
agencies.

1. General context
Gender equality is a fundamental value and a key goal of the EU. The elimination of inequalities between
women and men is essential for the creation of a stronger, fairer and more inclusive Europe. EU and EU
Member State policies recognise gender equality as a backbone of economic and social well-being and a
prerequisite for more inclusive societies. The policies that will guide the work of the European Institute for
Gender Equality (EIGE) during the 2026–2028 programming period reaffirm policy attention to gender
equality and the EU’s efforts towards more gender-responsive gains.
1.1. Policy context
In 2024, there was a leadership change in the EU. EU citizens went to the polls to vote in the European
Parliament (EP) elections and a new College of Commissioners then took up power. The EU political
priorities, accounting for the new challenges, are outlined in the 2024–2029 EU strategic agenda (2), the
2024–2029 Commission priorities (3) and other strategic documents. In line with the vision outlined in
these documents, progress in gender equality represents a significant yet underutilised asset for the EU,
capable of addressing the long-term challenges of growth and productivity amid declining populations, as
highlighted in the Draghi report The Future of European Competitiveness – A competitiveness strategy for
Europe (4). By advancing gender equality in education, training, the labour market and work–life balance
policies, the EU can further boost labour market participation, enhance work intensity and entrepreneurship
and more effectively tackle skills shortages and mismatches. This would not only lead to a sustained boost to
the EU’s economic productivity and innovation, but also foster greater social cohesion, help mitigate
demographic imbalances and further enhance the EU’s attractiveness to global talent, be it women or men in
all their diversity. It would reinforce the EU’s commitment to equity and social inclusion, ensuring that
economic progress is both sustainable and aligned with its core values.
In 2025, many of the major EU strategies, including the 2020–2025 EU gender equality strategy, the 2020–
2025 EU anti-racism action plan and the 2020–2025 LGBTIQ equality strategy (as part of a set of union of
equality strategies) ended. While these strategies have set the basis for a renewal of policy priorities and
policy continuity, the planning period of 2026–2028 is still within the time span of the 2020–2030 EU Roma
strategic framework for equality, inclusion and participation and the 2021–2030 strategy for the rights of
persons with disabilities. Gender equality is also one of the key principles of the European Pillar of Social
Rights, which calls for equality of treatment and opportunities between women and men in the labour
market in relation to terms and conditions of employment, career progression and the right to equal pay (5).
The European Pillar of Social Rights action plan, put forward by the Commission in March 2021, sets an EU
headline target to achieve an employment rate of at least 78 % among the population aged 20–64 by 2030
and to at least halve the gender employment gap compared with 2019. In 2023–2024, the EU accession to

The 2026–2028 programming period will build on the priorities indicated in the 2025–2027 single
programming document (SPD) and other EU strategic processes, which will include preparing relevant new
strategies, for example gender equality strategy, European democracy shield, LGBTIQ equality strategy, anti-
racism strategy, quality jobs roadmap, European Pillar of Social Rights action plan, anti-poverty strategy and
civil society strategy.
Specifically, EIGE’s programme for 2026–2028 is centred around the Commission’s priorities and goals:
• a new plan for Europe’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness;
• a new era for European defence and security;
• supporting people, strengthening our societies and our social model;
• sustaining our quality of life: food security, water and nature;
• protecting our democracy, upholding our values;
• a global Europe: leveraging our power and partnerships;
• delivering together and preparing our union for the future.
The rapidly changing geopolitical and security landscape, for example due to Russia’s war of aggression
against Ukraine, has increased the urgency of tackling various priorities simultaneously. The green transition
and energy security, economic turmoil and EU preparedness to support and integrate (war) refugees all
continue to be realities. A number of EU and national policies are in development to tackle these issues, and
gender equality should be at the core of policy responses. Given the gendered nature of the crises, marked
by increased risks of gender-based violence, trafficking of women and children, gender-unequal integration
into labour markets and strained care infrastructure and public services, gender-sensitive solutions are the
only sustainable way out. The European Commission’s response to these challenges will further guide EIGE’s
work in these areas, particularly on gender-based violence.
The roadmap on women’s rights and the gender equality strategy for 2026–2030 will remain
the main reference for the EU’s gender equality priorities in the coming years, guiding EIGE’s
focus during 2026–2028.
In line with its Founding Regulation, EIGE will continue to collect data, conduct research, develop tools and
provide technical support for gender mainstreaming, and make policy recommendations on gender equality
and communicate these to key stakeholders. The implementation of EU gender equality legislation and
strategies requires joint institutional responsibility, so EIGE will continue to provide high-quality data,
knowledge and technical support to contribute to the evidence-based policymaking of EU institutions and
Member States.
1.2. Gender equality challenges
EIGE planning for 2026–2028 takes into account both the changing policy context as indicated above and
recent challenges to and opportunities for gender equality. While insights on the gender equality challenges
pertaining to 2026–2028 and beyond are (being) gathered on the basis of various information sources, the
following sources are of particular importance to the multiannual planning:
• EIGE research and policy consultations, in the context of:
• Beijing Platform for Action + 30: the sixth review of the implementation of the Beijing

• EIGE strategic foresight work (ongoing since 2023).
In 2023–2024, EIGE conducted a strategic foresight exercise that aimed to analyse developments in
gender equality in the EU and highlight emerging trends. The Joint Research Centre (JRC) identified drivers
of change or megatrends that are relevant for the future of Europe (8); in line with these, EIGE’s strategic
foresight workshops and public opinion survey identified five key trends that are most impactful for future
developments in gender equality: digitalisation, the changing nature of work, climate change and the green
transition, diversifying inequalities and changing attitudes to, values of and threats to democratic institutions.
These five trends were further discussed with EIGE’s stakeholders in its second Gender Equality Forum in
December 2024 and confirmed as central.
Digitalisation and gender equality
This trend explores the double-edged sword of technological advancement, highlighting the potential for
digital tools to enhance accessibility and efficiency, while also acknowledging the risks of reinforcing gender
biases, exacerbating gender digital divides and increasing cybersecurity threats. Increasing digitalisation has
far-reaching implications for the roles of women and men and the most disadvantaged groups among them in
society. If anything, the COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the digital transition and amplified existing
trends in remote work, e-commerce and enhanced labour mobility. The age of hyper-connectivity impacts
forms of employment, career models and organisational structures. The digital divide is the fastest-growing
inequality, and it is not gender-neutral.
EIGE’s stakeholders engaged in strategic foresight identified a number of subtrends in relation to
digitalisation that will impact the future of gender equality, such as the following.
• AI and gender bias: AI-driven technologies can perpetuate and amplify gender biases present in their
training data, affecting opportunities in the labour market and social media algorithms.
• Cybersecurity and privacy: higher risks of cyberviolence, online harassment and privacy breaches are
often faced by women and marginalised groups.
• Remote work and connectivity: digital tools enable remote work, offering flexibility. At home, this
may improve work–life balance, but may also blur boundaries between work and personal life,
leading to burnout. These processes are closely linked to structural gender inequalities and may
deter or facilitate progress.
• Digital literacy and access: the gender digital divide affects access to information, services and
opportunities, which could further widen gender inequalities in education and economic
opportunities, including career prospects.
• E-government services: digitisation of public services can improve access, but also can exclude those
with a low level of, or no, digital skills or access.
• Access to accurate data: more access to more real-time data means that more decisions can be

The changing nature of work
This trend reflects the significant transformations in the labour market driven by the gig economy,
automation and remote work. While digitalisation and increased flexibility offer new opportunities in the
labour market, they also raise concerns about job security, equitable access to emerging jobs and the
recognition of unpaid care work, as the last one remains among the main barriers to women’s participation
in the labour market. Full-time equivalent (FTE) employment rates are consistently lower for women than
for men, with gender gaps being particularly large among couples with children.
The strategic foresight exercise identified several subtrends in relation to the changing nature of work and
its potential interlinks with gender equality, such as the following.
• Gig economy and precarious employment: the rise of gig work offers flexibility but lacks traditional
employment protection. Depending on gender biases in uptake of gig and precarious jobs, gender
gaps in access to social and financial security can amplify.
• Care economy transformation: this refers to shifts in who performs care work and how it is valued.
Within households, there is much more potential for more equitable distribution of unpaid domestic
and care work. In society, recognising and compensating care work would shift societal values
towards gender equality.
• Automation and job displacement: automation may threaten jobs in sectors with high levels of
female employment, while gender segregation and limited options to access training (e.g. due to
unpaid care) might limit women’s options for reskilling or upskilling.
• Workplace flexibility and culture: these refer to changing attitudes towards work–life balance and
flexible working hours/place. While, within households, this can support a more equitable division of
unpaid domestic and care work, in the labour market it requires cultural shifts to avoid penalising
those who utilise flexibility.
• Skills and education for the future workforce: continuous learning allows people to keep pace with
technological changes, which may pose numerous gendered barriers.
Climate change and the green transition
This trend recognises that climate change disproportionately affects women, through increased inequalities
and environmental degradation. However, it also presents unique opportunities for promoting gender
equality within the green transition towards an economy and society that is both environmentally sustainable
and gender-inclusive.
The strategic foresight exercise identified a number of subtrends in relation to climate change and the green
transition that are important with regard to gender equality, such as the following.
• Policy integration and gender-sensitive approaches: encouraging gender-responsive procurement,
budgeting and research to ensure gender equality and the green transition go hand in hand. In
society, for example, green and gender budgeting tools can lead to more sustainable and equitable
allocation of resources.
• Environmental degradation and vulnerability: this requires recognising that climate change
disproportionately impacts women and acting on it. For example, gender-specific health risks and
increased care demands from environmental degradation should lead to targeted health and social
support services.

• Climate change, migration and security: the EU faces significant risks from migration due to climate
change. For example, it is noted that climate migration heightens risks for women, including
increased sexual violence and trafficking.
• Sustainable urban and rural development: towns, cities and rural areas can be better designed to
support gender equality across different areas of life (i.e. employment, accessibility to services,
security).
Diversifying inequalities
This trend refers to a growing consensus that widening inequalities is an urgent issue that should top
policymakers’ agendas. It focuses on the intersectionality of gender with other characteristics, highlighting
how inequalities are compounded and often widening for individuals facing discrimination and disadvantages
along multiple axes, such as race, sexual orientation and disability. It emphasises the need for policies that
address these layered inequalities simultaneously.
The strategic foresight exercise identified a number of subtrends in relation to diversifying gender
inequalities, such as the following.
• Intersectionality and multiple identities: more attention needs to be paid to recognising the
compounded inequalities faced by individuals at the intersection of gender with race, sexual
orientation, disability and other household or individual characteristics.
• Economic/financial inequalities and access to resources: this refers to identifying and acting to reduce
gender disparities in earnings, income and wealth accumulation, including retirement income.
• Healthcare accessibility and quality: more attention needs to be paid to gender-specific health needs
and gender disparities in healthcare access and treatment.
• Education and skills development: gender gaps in education and vocational training, especially in
science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) and education, health and welfare fields,
are still large and barely reducing. Overcoming gender stereotypes in education is an essential factor
to bring about social and cultural changes.
Changing attitudes to, values of and new challenges for democratic institutions
This trend addresses the impact on gender equality of shifting political landscapes and societal attitudes. It
points to the challenges posed by rising populism and anti-gender equality movements. It is rooted in the
need for increased representation of women in leadership roles to ensure that gender perspectives are
integrated into governance and policymaking. It recognises the role that (social) media channels can play,
particularly in spreading disinformation at scale.
The strategic foresight exercise identified several subtrends in relation to changing attitudes to and values of
democratic institutions and the need to strengthen them, such as the following.
• Political representation and leadership: addressing the under-representation of women in political
and leadership positions. In society, this affects the prioritisation of gender equality in policy agendas.
At work, it influences organisational cultures and equality initiatives.
• Legislation and policy for gender equality: the evolution of laws and policies addressing gender
discrimination and promoting equality, including ensuring a more ‘integrated’ analysis of gender
issues in policymaking.
• Social movements and activism: the role of grassroots and global movements in advancing gender
equality, including global collaborations, generational changes in attitudes and allyship (e.g. with men,
with LGBTQIA+ issues and groups) and multipliers.

• Countering anti-equality narratives: developing narratives and tactics to reduce the effectiveness of
populist/anti-equality movements, including addressing the rise and spread of disinformation,
countering backlash against gender equality and women’s rights and countering challenges to
fundamental rights and democratic values.
• Sudden shocks to democratic systems: dealing with the disproportionate impacts of (unpredictable)
geopolitical and/or humanitarian crises, for example war, migration, pandemic and climate change.
• Cultural norms and media representation: the portrayal of gender in media and entertainment,
including social media, and its influence on societal attitudes. In society, such representation can
either reinforce stereotypes or promote inclusive narratives.
1.3. EIGE’s response to the policy context and gender equality
challenges
The 2020–2025 gender equality strategy, the Task Force on Equality and the Commission’s commitment to
gender equality and gender mainstreaming within relevant portfolios have all increased the need for EIGE’s
evidence-based information and resources on gender equality, and for technical assistance in implementing
gender equality, particularly gender mainstreaming.
Due to growing recognition of the Gender Equality Index as a monitoring tool to assess gender equality
progress in the EU, the Index has been released annually since 2019. The EU gender equality strategy for
2020–2025 recognises the Index as a key benchmark for gender equality and has established a Gender
Equality Strategy Monitoring Portal (9) that builds on the Index. This adds high political relevance to annual
Index releases. Since 2019, the Index has focused on a theme of high political relevance (work–life balance in
2019, digitalisation and the future of work in 2020, health in 2021, care and the COVID-19 pandemic in
2022, the European Green Deal in 2023 violence against women in 2024 and gender stereotypes in 2025).
This allows for a broader context for interpretation of Index scores and more comprehensive analysis
of gender inequalities in selected areas. The thematic focus also presents key indicators to monitor
progress in gender equality in related policy areas. Ten years after its first release in 2013, the Index was
conceptually and methodologically updated. The revised edition was launched in 2025. In 2026 the Index will
focus on the theme of parental leave policies in the EU.
In 2024, EIGE carried out the second wave of the EU-wide Survey of Gender Gaps in Unpaid Care,
Individual and Social Activities (CARE survey). The data was presented in the 2025 Gender Equality
Index and the thematic reports responding to broader policy needs. The third wave of the survey will take
place in 2027, subject to budget availability. The overall objective of the survey is to fill the data gaps in the
EU policy priority areas of work–life balance, gender inequalities in informal care and access to care services.
The survey covers several thematic areas: informal long-term care, informal childcare, access to care
services, housework, leisure, volunteering/charitable/political activities, work–life balance, gender norms,
health and well-being, means of transport used, use of digital tools and environmental considerations,
including in caring activities. Since 2023, the survey data has improved the capacity of the Gender Equality
Index to capture changes in the domain of time in a conceptually sound, coherent and regular way. This EU-
wide data contributed to monitoring the 2020–2025 gender equality strategy (10), for which closing the

Since 2010, the presidencies of the Council of the European Union have requested EIGE’s

reports focusing on BPfA implementation support the presidency of the first semester while the thematic

The research support to the presidencies enables EIGE to work on priority policy issues, such as emerging
gender equality outcomes of the COVID-19 crisis (2020–2021), gender inequalities in AI and platform work
(2020–2021), psychological violence against women and coercive control (2021–2022), young women and
men in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic (2021–2022), gender equality and gender mainstreaming in
the COVID-19 recovery (2022–2023), work–life balance: bridging the gender care gap (2022–2023), gender
inequality and financial independence (2023–2024), return to the labour market after parental leave (2024),
gender stereotypes (2025) and cyberviolence affecting girls (2025–2026). In 2025, EIGE published the review
Beijing Platform for Action + 30, making another important contribution to the assessment of progress in
gender equality across the 12 areas of the BPfA since 2019. The review presented recommendations on
possible policy actions to promote gender equality after 2025 and strengthen the monitoring of gender
equality in the EU. It also informed the EU position on the global assessment of progress in the situation of
women and gender equality and empowerment of women and girls (as carried out, for example, by the
Commission on the Status of Women). In 2026–2027, EIGE will carry out a study titled ‘Breaking barriers,
building resilience in the EU: gender equality for a future-ready workforce’ in support of the Lithuanian
Presidency (2027).
Building on its extensive experience in work–life balance and informal care, EIGE will continue to support
the monitoring of work–life balance and care-related policy initiatives and measures across
the EU by providing relevant data (e.g. CARE survey) and informing policy discussions. Together with the
European Commission’s Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers (DG Justice and Consumers) and
the JRC, EIGE will continue to support updates of the Gender Equality Strategy Monitoring Portal (12).

Activity 5. Research and development of the indicators on gender-based violence: female
genital mutilation and femicide
The 2020–2025 EU gender equality strategy recognised FGM, forced abortion, forced sterilisation, early and
forced marriage, so-called honour-related violence and other harmful practices against women and girls as
forms of gender-based violence and serious violations of women’s and children’s rights in the EU and around
the world. Ending FGM was a key action point under the 2020–2024 EU action plan on human rights and
democracy and the 2021–2025 EU gender action plan and is an integral part of the directive on combating
violence against women and domestic violence.
Building on EIGE’s previous work on FGM and femicide, this activity will support the implementation of the
directive on combating violence against women and domestic violence and the Commission’s (proposed)
recommendation to prevent and tackle harmful practices by initiating research and exploring methods and
developing indicators for Member States to systematically collect data on harmful practices against women
and girls.
Contributing to strategic objectives
• Contribute to better-informed and evidence-based policymaking and decision-making to achieve gender equality and fight
harmful practices against women and girls
• Effectively promote gender equality to key stakeholders and target groups
Specific objective(s): to support the development of a comparable measurement framework on violence against women by
providing the tools to collect reliable data on harmful practices at the EU and Member State levels
Overview of the activity
Building on its previous work on developing conceptual and measurement frameworks on specific forms of violence against
women (e.g. intimate partner violence, femicide, cyberviolence against women and girls, FGM) and to support the implementation
of the directive on combating violence against women together with the Commission’s recommendation to prevent and tackle
harmful practices, EIGE will assess the possibility of extending the data collection to specific forms of violence against women and
harmful practices, such as FGM and femicide. In 2026–2028, EIGE will focus on research for measuring specific forms of harmful
practices against women and girls, paying particular attention to FGM. EIGE will test the updated step-by-step methodological
guide (third edition), to ensure a more accurate estimate of FGM-related practices. The new edition of the step-by-step guide will
aim to be a practical support for those appointed the task of estimating the risk of FGM in a region or a country within the EU.
Furthermore, EIGE aims to establish new ways to observe the prevalence of femicide at the EU level and to continue to explore
additional avenues for data collection from an intersectional perspective (e.g. liaising with non-governmental organisations (NGOs)
active in the field of LGBTQIA+ rights or NGOs focused on sexual violence and trafficking for sexual exploitation).
Expected results
EIGE’s ongoing work on administrative data collection on violence against women aims to establish a standardised measurement
framework to collect comparable data at the EU level. The measurement of violence against women should also advance the
collection of data on harmful practices. The expected results of this activity are as follows:
1. updated methodology for estimating the prevalence of FGM across Member States;
2. examined new approaches for reporting on femicide and good practices for prevention across Member States.
Main outputs
EIGE will provide mapping of different definitions, available data sources and statistical products for indicators on femicide. As part

Activity 6. Research on emerging issue(s): gender-based violence in times of crisis
EIGE’s work on gender-based violence in times of crisis started with an assessment of the increased risk of
intimate partner violence as a consequence of COVID-19-related lockdown policies. The research found
that the prevalence and severity of gender-based violence, particularly sexual and domestic violence, are
exacerbated in crisis settings. It also showed that an increase in violence during the COVID-19 pandemic
could be projected to other crises, such as civil conflicts, natural disasters and climate change. For example,
Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine posed a new crisis scenario in the EU, with significant
displacement and many women and children from Ukraine exposed to heightened levels of sexual violence.
EIGE’s research confirms that gender inequalities are exacerbated in conflict settings.
To ensure comprehensive, high-quality and impactful research, EIGE will work closely with EU agencies
working in this field (e.g. EUAA, Eurojust, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency) and international
organisations (e.g. OSCE, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees), strengthening collaboration on gender
and migration.
Contributing to strategic objectives
• Contribute to better-informed and evidence-based policymaking and decision-making to achieve gender equality and fight
discrimination based on sex
• Effectively promote gender equality to key stakeholders and target groups
Specific objective(s): to complement the work of EU institutions and international organisations ensuring that women and girls
fleeing conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence in specific settings can exercise their rights and receive gender-sensitive,
trauma-oriented and victim-centred support and care in transit and reception centres; to support the monitoring of the
implementation of the Istanbul Convention, especially Articles 60 and 61; to collect data on gender-based violence of women and
girls in transit and reception centres
Overview of the activity
In 2025, EIGE published the findings on Member States’ measures, policies, guidelines and national action plans, especially those
related to UN Resolution 1325, to assess policy gaps for migrant, refugee, and asylum seeker victims of gender-based violence. In
2026, EIGE plans to analyse the implementation of the Istanbul Convention provisions on gender-based asylum claims and non-
refoulement. The project will build on its previous work identifying national and EU-wide policies, guidelines and actions plans on
the gender aspects of refugees and asylum seekers arriving in the EU. The new project will take a closer look at how these
policies and guidelines are implemented at transit and reception centres, focusing on the operationalisation of gender-based
violence screenings. Article 60(3) of the Istanbul Convention will serve as a reference point, ‘Parties shall take the necessary
legislative or other measures to develop gender-sensitive reception procedures and support services for asylum-seekers as well as
gender guidelines and gender-sensitive asylum procedures, including refugee status determination and application for international
protection.’ Given the sensitivity of the topic, EIGE will work closely with experts from European and international organisations,
such as the EUAA and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, with ethical and security questions at the centre of the research
design. Semi-structured, in-depth interviews will seek to gain a comprehensive overview of the implementation of gender-sensitive
and victim-oriented screenings at reception centres. Research participants will be humanitarian workers, reception centre staff,
officers, volunteers and relevant professionals, NGOs dealing with women and girl refugees and asylum seekers and, if possible,
victims who have passed through reception centres. Building on the findings of the previous year, reports by the Group of Experts
on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence and the interviews, EIGE will develop practical guidance on
how best to implement gender-based violence screening and apply Articles 60 and 61 of the Istanbul Convention, enabling

EIGE’s 2026 activity will further build on the 2024–2025 work to increase awareness of potential gaps in the implementation of

recommendations in the area of gender-sensitive screenings at reception centres, (2) increase awareness of the need to
implement victim- and trauma-oriented screening for women and girls fleeing crisis so that they can receive adequate
psychological support, justice and legal status, and create functioning, efficient and up-to-date referral systems and (3) support

Activity 9. Gender Statistics Database
EIGE’s Gender Statistics Database is a centralised, reliable and up-to-date source of key gender statistics and
indicators. It aims to assist EU institutions and Member States by collating, analysing and communicating
reliable and comparable data on equality between women and men, thereby improving the quality,
production and availability of gender statistics. It also provides a platform to disseminate developments in
the field of gender statistics. EIGE ensures that the database is maintained as a key source of reference data
on gender statistics, updated regularly, user-friendly and accessible.

In 2026, the Gender Statistics Database will focus on providing continuity to statistical data collection, for which EIGE is a

commitment to integrating a gender perspective into all major initiatives to ensure that policies and programmes maximise
the potential of women and men, girls and boys, in all their diversity. Appropriate disaggregation will gradually be
introduced into the database to expand the intersectional approach across EIGE’s activities and the monitoring of key EU

serve as an avenue to present EIGE’s evidence, positioned within broader topics and issues, and to explore storytelling
approaches to reach wider audiences and encourage stakeholder and public engagement. Campaigns will be implemented in close
cooperation with the EP, the European Commission and other key communication multipliers, including the C10 group. They will
apply both gender and intersecting inequalities perspectives.
EIGE will continue to reach out to broader audiences, particularly young people. By strengthening the understandings of the need
for gender equality, EIGE can help to maintain a key value underpinning societies in the EU today and in the future. EIGE will
continue to explore the use of various communication channels and tools to reach these audiences, for example by refreshing its
presence on social media channels or adopting new formats.
While EIGE will integrate its evidence into its communication campaigns, specific communication and monitoring will be used for
relevant projects and evidence.
In 2026, EIGE will continue to engage with media at the EU and national levels to strengthen reporting on gender equality.
Beyond the reactive response to media queries, it aims to develop more proactive engagement through its established networks
and through timely interaction with key media outlets and influential voices responding to current topics and developments.
There is a continued backlash against gender equality and women’s rights, fuelled by gender-based mis- and disinformation. As the
European knowledge centre on gender equality, EIGE continues to play its role in developing knowledge on better ways to
communicate gender equality topics, both in policymaking contexts and in the broader public discourse. In 2026, EIGE will
continue its Comms Lab activities to provide a platform for exchange (community of practice), learning and joint testing of
communication approaches.
In 2026, EIGE will organise its third Gender Equality Forum. EIGE will continue activities to strengthen the Agency’s crisis
preparedness and response, and to increase the ability of key staff to present findings in effective and engaging ways to the

EIGE expects to engage stakeholders and the wider public through communication campaigns that foster an evidence-based
public discussion on important issues for gender equality. It will maintain EIGE’s media coverage and social media outreach, in line
with the results of the latest baseline (see the table below). EIGE intends to be the first reference point for policymakers,
decision-makers, experts, journalists and citizens searching for information and resources on gender equality.

Communication campaign(s) aim to raise awareness and/or change attitudes related to selected thematic priorities by highlighting
EIGE’s work and evidence. Using digital communications through EIGE’s website and proactive media engagement, each campaign
and related communication approaches will provide an easy-to-understand explanation of key research findings and evidence.
Audiovisual and visual products and editorial content will present information creatively and concisely and explore storytelling
approaches. EIGE’s social media posts on relevant social media platform(s) will raise awareness of key gender equality issues and

equality conversations, including the backlash against gender equality and anti-gender narratives. It supports stakeholders to

Activity 13. Increased capacity of EU candidates and a potential candidate in the Western
Balkans and Türkiye to monitor and mainstream gender equality (2024–2027)
On 15 July 2025 the Agency and DG Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood signed Contract
No 700003298 under the Commission implementing decision on the financing of the multi-country annual
action plan in favour of the Western Balkans and Türkiye for 2024, action document for ‘EU4 social
inclusion’. The implementation period of the action is 48 months.
The action contributes to the European Commission action document for ‘EU4 social inclusion’
implementing the multi-country annual action plan in favour of the Western Balkans and Türkiye, financed
under IPA III. It is aligned with the EU gender action plan III for 2021–2025 and the IPA III programming
framework, both of which emphasise the importance of mainstreaming gender equality as a cross-cutting
issue. It is also directly relevant to SDG 5 (gender equality).
The overall objective of the action is to facilitate the effective participation of the EU candidate countries
and a potential candidate country in the Western Balkans and Türkiye in EIGE’s activities upon EU
accession, by supporting their alignment with the EU acquis in the area of gender equality. The action will
focus on continuing and building on the results of the previous EIGE cooperation with the beneficiaries
under the IPA since 2013, adjusting to stakeholders’ needs, the objectives outlined in the EU enlargement
package and the Commission’s Western Balkans strategy.
Contributing to strategic objectives
• Contribute to better-informed and evidence-based policymaking and decision-making to achieve gender equality and fight
discrimination based on sex
• Effectively promote gender equality to key stakeholders and target groups
Specific objective(s)
• Specific objective 1: IPA beneficiaries are further integrated into core areas of EIGE’s work programme and have an
increased ability to monitor and mainstream gender equality, including to develop and independently maintain national
gender equality indices
• Specific objective 2: IPA beneficiaries have strengthened their capacities in the collection of data on violence against women
in alignment with Directive (EU) 2024/1385 on combating violence against women and domestic violence
• Specific objective 3: IPA beneficiaries participate effectively in the Regional Coordination Platform for Gender Equality
Action
Overview of the activity
EIGE has implemented IPA projects since 2013. This is the sixth IPA project. The project aims to contribute to beneficiary
countries’ progress towards the adoption of the EU acquis on gender equality, an aim that is nearly self-evident given that the
acquis is a legal prerequisite for EU accession. It focuses on continuing and building on the results of the previous project, that
is, maintaining strong regional cooperation and aligning the project with gender equality needs in the beneficiary countries.
The activity aims to further integrate EU candidate countries and potential candidate countries into EIGE’s core work areas and
to continue to foster regional cooperation on gender equality. The following activities will contribute to achieving the project
objectives and outputs in 2026:
• EIGE will support up to two IPA beneficiaries in calculating and releasing national gender equality indices and will
organise a workshop to introduce the 2025 Gender Equality Index updates and thematic focuses;
• EIGE will assess the feasibility of conducting EIGE’s CARE survey in IPA III beneficiaries, to ensure that the necessary
data are available for the Gender Equality Index domain of time;
• EIGE’s Gender Statistics Database will include data from the IPA beneficiaries on women and men in decision-making;
• EIGE will introduce its latest gender mainstreaming tools and methods to the IPA beneficiaries;
• EIGE will launch the mapping of the sources of administrative data on violence against women and domestic violence
in the IPA beneficiaries;
• up to two regional coordination meetings will continue to bring together representatives from IPA beneficiaries;
• experts from IPA beneficiaries will be invited to attend relevant meetings and thematic events (e.g. conferences,
working groups, study visits, thematic networks and experts’ meetings) organised by EIGE;

Annex 6. Environment management
EIGE remains committed to ensuring that its contracts include environmentally sustainability clauses. To
date, EIGE has included the requirements of environmental measures in contracts covering the following:
• stationery and printing materials,
• cleaning services,
• delivery and installation of office furniture,
• production of promotional materials,
• catering services,
• organisation of events.
EIGE provides measures for recycling food waste, paper and plastic. An example of this is EIGE’s successful
bottles for charity programme. A reduction in the amount of printing paper used is actively encouraged. To
achieve this, EIGE’s default printing option is set to duplex format in black and white, and shared printers
are fitted with staff ID card readers. In 2023, electronic workflows replaced paper-based workflows entirely.
During induction training, EIGE’s commitment to environmentally friendly work practices is highlighted to
new staff.
EIGE’s missions management tool includes an electronic workflow for mission approval and reporting
(mission reports). It also collects data on carbon dioxide (CO ) emissions for business travel, as provided by
2
the travel agent.
In 2024, EIGE’s mission-related CO emissions amounted to 85 tonnes. The Agency reinforced the mission
2
pre-approval process, which considers possibilities for online participation, and the need for in-person
meetings over remote participation must be justified. EIGE intends to remain below 100 tonnes of CO
2
emissions in 2026.
Following the new rental contract for EIGE’s premises in Vilnius, the Internal Refurbishment Committee was
set up to process the design and overview the works carried out to improve the office space. This includes
using environmentally sustainable refurbishment materials (e.g. Ecolabel paint, furniture made from recycled
materials), introducing green spaces (e.g. green wall and mini-garden area) and using appliances with the
most efficient energy rating according to the EU energy label (A+++). In addition, EIGE’s premises now
includes signs encouraging colleagues to use the stairs instead of the elevator.
EIGE’s Green Officer will propose targets for further reductions in the carbon footprint from business
travel in the programming period. Travelling to work has also been addressed through a pilot summer
programme called green commute, which aimed to educate colleagues and reduce their daily CO footprint
2
when travelling to work. This was achieved by promoting modes of transport such as walking, cycling, public
transport and carpooling.
Overall, the main tasks of the Green Officer in 2026 will be to:
• discuss and agree on environmentally relevant indicators;
• achieve the targets to reduce the negative impacts of EIGE’s operations;
• propose additional green measures;
• raise staff awareness of environmental sustainability.

Annex 9. Evaluations
A. External evaluations
In line with Article 20 of its Founding Regulation, EIGE’s management board commissions the organisation of
the external evaluations of the Agency.
The second evaluation of EIGE took place in 2022. The evaluation report (33) was presented at the
November 2022 management board meeting.
According to the external evaluation, EIGE is a well-functioning organisation and fulfils the mandate set out
in its Founding Regulation. Its expertise and programme of work are key in the promotion of gender equality
in the EU, and its data and research are needed to ensure and inform further progress. Stakeholders value
EIGE’s contribution to the development of effective policies and initiatives. The Gender Equality Index
continues to be the main reference on gender equality within the EU, providing a platform to compare
Member States and monitor gender equality.
The report shows considerable improvement since the first evaluation of EIGE in 2015. Nevertheless, some
key concerns persist, such as the role of the Experts’ Forum, the functioning of the management board and
staffing issues.

Annex 10. Strategy for organisational management and the
internal control system
EIGE’s internal control system aims to assure the appropriate management of risks relating to the legality
and regularity of the underlying transactions and the nature of payments. It is designed to provide reasonable
assurance in achieving effectiveness, efficiency and economy of operations; reliability of reporting;
safeguarding of assets and information; and prevention, detection, correction and follow-up of fraud and
irregularities.
The internal control system is based on segregation of duties, a risk management and control strategy,
avoidance of conflicts of interest, appropriate audit trails and data integrity in data systems and established
procedures for monitoring performance and following up internal control weaknesses.
On 12 June 2019, EIGE’s management board adopted a new internal control framework in line with the
revised internal control framework of the European Commission. Seventeen principles are set out to
provide assurance in meeting the organisation’s objectives. Specific assessments will be conducted annually
during 2026–2028, in accordance with the assessment methodology.
A main internal control objective in the programming period is the implementation of all audit
recommendations in line with the relevant action plans. A related objective is to carry out ex post controls
on financial transactions. EIGE has already made all preparations to carry out these inspections in-house.
This activity began in 2021 and will be performed annually in the programming period.
A second objective is the implementation of the 2024–2026 anti-fraud strategy. The strategy will
contribute to strengthening the anti-fraud system in EIGE and enhancing its internal control system. EIGE
will also conduct training on ethics and integrity, fraud prevention and management of conflicts of interest. In
2026, a thorough fraud risk assessment will be performed in preparation for the anti-fraud strategy for
2027–2029.
A third objective is the implementation of the conflicts of interest policy and of the actions set out in that
policy, namely, annual screening of the declarations of interest of the management board and Experts’ Forum
members, management of potential conflicts of interest of external experts engaged following a publication
of a call for expressions of interest and assessment and management of potential conflicts of interest for
staff not covered by the EU Staff Regulations. As regards transparency requirements, EIGE will publish
monthly on its website the Director’s meetings with interest representatives, in accordance with Director’s
Decision No 316 of 25 June 2024 on the publication of Director’s meetings with interest representatives
and guidelines on the use of the Transparency Register.

Annex 12. Strategy for cooperation with non-EU countries and/or international organisations
EIGE works with international organisations and non-EU countries at different levels: (1) special projects, (2) ad hoc cooperation, (3) regular information exchange
and (4) promoting its work.
1. Special projects are subject to external funding, such as EIGE’s cooperation with the EU candidate and potential candidate countries, which is funded by DG
Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood.
2. Ad hoc cooperation is subject to the Director’s decision and agreement with DG Justice and Consumers. It may involve organisation of joint events, or sharing
data or expertise, with the view that it contributes to or promotes the work done by EIGE.
3. Information exchange is coordinated by the Outreach and Engagement Unit. It involves participating and contributing to working groups and meetings of key
international organisations, such as the Council of Europe’s Gender Equality Commission or the Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women
and Domestic Violence. EIGE organises regular information exchanges with its key partners to ensure that partners are aware of each other’s work and
contribute to that work where appropriate.
4. EIGE promotes its work at the international level through regular communication channels or presentations at events organised by international organisations.
